The term *vākyaśeṣa* (supplementation of a sentence) refers to that which, for the sake of brevity, is not explicitly stated as a word by the teacher in a sentence but is supplied by virtue of being understood. For example, in the phrase "the activity of causal factors," the word "exists" (*asti*) is supplied; likewise, in the phrase "with juices born of arid lands," the word "meat" (*māṃsa*) is supplied. Furthermore, these very words are treated as supplements in sentences when they are understood even though they have not been inserted.

The term *prayojana* (purpose) refers to that object for the sake of which one acts with desire; for example: "The equalization of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) is stated to be the purpose of this treatise."
*Upadeśa* (instruction) is the teaching of an authoritative person (*āpta*); for example: "One should first apply oleation (*sneha*), and immediately thereafter, sudation (*sveda*)," and so forth.

*Apadeśa* (reasoning) is the statement of a reason (*hetu*) for the purpose of establishing the matter proposed (*pratijñāta-artha*); for example: "One should know [the origin] from wind, from water, from place, from time, and from inherent nature (*svabhāva*), because they are unavoidable (*duṣparihāryatvāt*)," and so forth. In this context, the statement of the reason for the proposed matter is: "because they are unavoidable."

*Atideśa* (extended application) is defined as a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that whatever has been explained for one purpose should be understood to apply similarly to other cases in order to establish unstated meanings; for example: "And whatever else may exist here that is not mentioned but is honored, Ātreya always approves of that as well.

*Arthāpatti* (presumption) is that which follows by implication from what is not explicitly stated; for example, when there is a prohibition against eating curd at night, it follows by implication that one should eat it during the day.

*Nirṇaya* (conclusion) is the final determination of a matter after it has been investigated; for example, having conducted an investigation into the fourfold nature of medicine and so forth, it is stated: "That which was described in the previous chapter as the sixteen-fold medicine is sufficient for health when applied with proper reasoning."

"Prasaṅga" (consequential repetition) is the restatement of a previously stated point because it has entered into the context or for some other reason; for example, after stating at the outset, "In that regard, excessive application [of the senses] consists in the seeing of visible objects by those of extreme brilliance beyond measure," he later restates that very same point with the words, "And from hearing excessively loud sounds in every way," and so forth.

The term *ekānta* (certainty) refers to that which is stated with definitive restriction; for example: "Intrinsic [disease] arises from bodily defects," or "Trivṛt causes purgation," and so forth. The term *anaikānta* (uncertainty) refers to the non-restriction of either one of two alternatives; for example: "Those patients who die despite being without medicine—would they all necessarily have recovered had they been provided with medicine? and so forth.

Exclusion (*apavarga*) is the removal of a specific part from that which has been prescribed in its entirety; for example: "One should not eat stale food, except for meat, green vegetables, dried vegetables, fruits, and edible delicacies. For here, having established a general prohibition against eating stale food, the consumption of meat and so forth—even if stale—is specifically exempted by being singled out. Contrariety (*viparyaya*) is an illustrative example to the contrary of what was excluded; for example: "The things mentioned in the etiology do not agree with him, while their opposites do agree."

The *pūrvapakṣa* (prior position) is a statement that subverts the meaning of the proposition asserted; for example, regarding the proposition "one should not eat fish with milk," the statement "one should indeed eat all kinds of fish with milk, except for the cilicima" [subverts it].

The author of the Sūtra, having established the rule, describes it as follows: "The channels of excretion are obstructed by vitiated humors (doṣas) that have exceeded their proper measure. In this context, by the word *duṣṭi* (vitiation), the Teacher intends both the deficiency and the excess of the humors; he explains this: "One should recognize the increase of the humors by heaviness, and their depletion by lightness, as well as by excessive retention or discharge from the channels of excretion."

Some, however, say that *vidhāna* (prescription) is the statement of a subject matter according to the sequence of the topics, such as the description of the production of plasma, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen in accordance with their order of formation. *Anumata* (consent) is the act of assenting by not refuting the opinion of a particular school; for example, after presenting the opinion of a certain school—such as "some say that the procedure for inducing the expulsion of the placenta in the case of a fetus that is a 'thorn' is palliative"—it is consented to by not prohibiting it.

Explanation (*vyākhyāna*) is that which explains what is not an object of ordinary cognition, such as: "In the first month, the embryo is coagulated, defiled by all the elements, consisting of phlegm, with an unmanifest form," and so forth—the explanation of matters unknown to people like us.

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition regarding two objects that are not yet determined, characterized by a desire for specific distinction, such as the doubt expressed in: "Some consider the mother and father to be the cause of birth; others [consider] inherent nature, the creation of another, or chance. And so forth.

*Atītāvekṣaṇa* (reference to the past) is that which refers only to what has already occurred; for example: "That hut and that bed also pacify fever," where one refers to the past huts and other items prescribed in the chapter on sudation (*sveda*). *Anāgatāvekṣaṇa* (reference to the future) is the accomplishment of a purpose by taking a future procedure as authoritative; for example: "Or else, [one may use] bitter ghee," and so forth, which is stated by way of reference to the future. *Svasaṃjñā* (technical term) is the name assigned by the authors of the treatises for the sake of conventional usage; for example, *jentāka*, *holāka*, and so forth, are technical terms.

*Ūhya* (that which is to be inferred) refers to that which is not explicitly stated in the text but is taught as something to be reasoned out through wisdom; for example: "Whatever substance, even if enumerated, one considers to be non-essential, that one should omit.
*Samuccaya* (conjunction) refers to that which is prescribed by way of combining this and that; for example: "The color and the accent," and so forth.
*Nidarśana* (illustration) refers to an example that serves as a common ground for the understanding of both the ignorant and the learned; for example: "Just as the nectar is known," and so forth.

An etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) is an illustration accessible to the intellect of the learned; for example: "The cause of the passing away of time is known, as if it were something ever-moving."

This is the distinction between illustration (*nidarśana*) and etymological explanation (*nirvacana*): an illustration is a subject of common understanding for both the ignorant and the learned, whereas an etymological explanation is to be known only by the intellect of the scholar; alternatively, *nirvacana* means etymology—as in: "Because it creeps (*sarpati*) in various ways (*vividham*), it is designated as *visarpa*," and so forth. *Niyoga* refers to an injunction (*vidhāna*) that must necessarily be carried out—as in: "Even when overcome by sweat and fainting, this bolus (*piṇḍikā*) must not be released by you," and so forth. *Vikalpa* is a statement of alternatives—as in: "Either *sāra* water or *kuśa* water," and so forth.

*Pratyutsāra* is the refutation of another's position by means of a logical argument (*upapatti*). For example, Vāryovida said: "Beings are born from *rajas*, and diseases are known to arise from *rajas*" and so forth; Hiraṇyākṣa refutes this, saying: "The self is certainly not known to be born of *rajas*" and so forth.

*Uddhāra* is the establishment of one's own position after having critiqued the opposing side. For example, the establishment of one's own position through such statements as: "Indeed, those very same conditions that produce prosperity for a man, those very same conditions bring about misfortune and diseases."

"Occurrence" (sambhava) means that when something arises in a particular place, that is its occurrence; for example, moles, freckles, and dark spots occur on the face, and so forth. Thus, these thirty-six methodological principles of the treatise (tantrayukti) have been explained.

Bhaṭṭāra Haricandra, however, has stated four other *tantrayuktis* called *paripraśna*, *vyākaraṇa*, *vyutkrāntābhidhāna*, and *hetu*; since these are not recited in the *Tantra*, they must be included within these very [sixteen]. Among them, *paripraśna* is included in *uddeśa*, while *vyākaraṇa* is included in *vyākhyāna*. *Vyutkrāntābhidhāna* is a variety of *nirdeśa*. By the word *hetu*, those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) that were mentioned are included under *hetu*.

The commentary consists of fifteen types, seven kinds of conceptualization, twenty-one bases of meaning, seventeen habitual tendencies, and fourteen defects of the system; since these have been explained in the *Uttaratantra*, they were not written down here by the Teacher. ||41-44||
For all these indeed exist in their entirety within the tantra taught both in brief and in detail. ||45||

Just as the sun [is seen] for only a portion of a lotus grove, or a lamp [is seen] for only a portion of a house, so too [the *tantrayuktis*] are seen only partially when they are expressed in an abbreviated form (*samāsābhihita*) within the treatise. Now, having enumerated the *tantrayuktis*, he explains their application specifically within the treatise, beginning with the words "In a treatise where [the subject] is stated both in brief and in detail" (*tantre samāsavyāsokte*). By the phrase "when expressed in an abbreviated form," he demonstrates that not all *tantrayuktis* necessarily occur in a treatise that is extremely concise; or rather, the connection is that they are seen only partially when expressed in an abbreviated form. (45) Just as the sun [illuminates] a lotus grove, or a lamp [illuminates] a house... (46)

The logical principles (*tantrayukti*) of the treatise serve the purpose of awakening and illumination. (47) Demonstrating the function of the *tantrayuktis* by means of an illustration, he says "just as" (*yathā*), and so forth. Just as the sun is the expander of a contracted lotus grove, so too the *tantrayuktis* are the expanders of the condensed portions of meaning within the treatise; he shows by the analogy of the sun that they become expanders through the act of awakening.

By means of the analogy of the lamp, however, it is shown that just as a lamp illuminates that which already exists but is concealed by darkness, so too do the methodological principles (*tantrayukti*) of the system illuminate a meaning that already exists but is hidden. With reference to these two objectives to be accomplished by the methodological principles, it is said: "They serve for the purpose of awakening and illumination. (46) "One whose intellect has found its footing here, even in this single treatise... (47)
Because he knows the underlying logic, he quickly masters even other treatises;
yet a physician who studies the scriptures without the *tantrayukti* does not grasp the meaning of those texts, just as one fails to obtain wealth when fortune has run out. (48)
He states the fruit of the proper study of the treatise: "Even in a single [verse]," and so forth. (47–48)
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the methodological principles of the treatise (tantrayukti). ||1||
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari said: ||2||

Following the section on the regimen for the healthy (*svasthavṛtta*), the chapter on the *tantrayukti*s (the principles of systematization) begins—starting with "Now, therefore" (*athātaḥ*) and so forth. The phrase "now, therefore" is to be explained as before. That by which one protects the body is the *tantra*—namely, the treatise (*śāstra*) and medical treatment (*cikitsā*). The *yukti*s of that [treatise] are its applications; these are the *tantrayukti*s. This chapter is composed concerning them. Here, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is elided, as in the case of the word *vedotpatti*.

And those applications of the tantra are of two kinds: application of the words (*vākyayojanā*) and application of the meaning (*arthayojanā*). Among these, application of the words consists of the presentation and explanation of the yoga, and so forth; application of the meaning consists of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), the meanings of the terms (*padārtha*), and so forth. ||1-2||
There are thirty-two methodological principles (*tantrayukti*) in the treatise.

They are as follows: the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*), connection (*yoga*), the meaning of the term (*padārtha*), the meaning of the reason (*hetvartha*), enumeration (*uddeśa*), detailed exposition (*nirdeśa*), instruction (*upadeśa*), indirect indication (*apadeśa*), partial application (*pradeśa*), extended application (*atideśa*), exclusion (*apavarja*), the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), contrariety (*viparyaya*), logical consequence (*prasaṅga*), the absolute (*ekānta*), the non-absolute (*anekānta*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final determination (*nirṇaya*), approval (*anumata*), prescription (*vidhāna*), anticipation of what is yet to come (*anāgatāvekṣaṇa*), reference to what has already passed (*atikrāntāvekṣaṇa*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), explanation (*vyākhyāna*), technical terminology (*svasañjñā*), etymological derivation (*nirvacana*), illustration (*nidarśana*), injunction (*niyoga*), and option (*vikalpa*).
The collection; it is to be inferred. ||3||

Pointing out the *tantrayukti*s by way of their numerical classification, he says: "thirty-two," and so forth. In the *Sauśruta* treatise, the number thirty-two is obtained simply from the enumeration of the items to be counted, such as "subject matter" (*adhikaraṇa*) and the rest; therefore, its formulation [here] is according to what is stated in other treatises.

The phrase "thirty-six or forty" is intended to preclude a fixed number of *tantrayukti*s (methodological principles). Regarding the word "in the treatise" (*śāstre*), others read it as "by way of summary" (*samāsena*) and explain it thus: elsewhere [the treatises] state thirty-six or forty *tantrayukti*s in detail; here, however, thirty-two are stated by way of summary. He asks, "Which are those *tantrayukti*s? and replies with "as follows," etc. "As follows" (*tadyathā*) indicates an illustration. The author of the aphorisms himself will explain the categories such as the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth. ||3||
What is the purpose of these tantrayuktis (methodological principles of the treatise)? It is said: the arrangement of sentences and the arrangement of meanings. (4)

Having thus presented the *tantrayukti*s by way of enumeration, he states their purpose with the words "In this [work]," and so forth. "In this" refers to the science of medicine (*cikitsāśāstra*). "Composition of sentences" (*vākyayojana*) and "composition of meanings" (*arthayojana*): the composition of sentences is the joining or connecting of sentences that were previously disconnected; the composition of meanings is the illumination and harmonization of meanings that were hidden or inconsistent. Among these, the purpose of certain *tantrayukti*s—such as *yoga*, *uddeśa*, and *nirdeśa*—is the composition of sentences, while for others—such as *adhikaraṇa*, *padārtha*, and *uddhṛta*—it is the composition of meanings. (4)
And there are verses on this point:

"The refutation of the statements employed by proponents of false doctrines, as well as the establishment of one's own statements, is accomplished through the methodological principles of the treatise (tantrayukti). (5)
Furthermore, those meanings which were not explicitly stated, those which were hidden, those which were impure, and those which were mentioned only briefly— all these shall now be established.

Right here, in order to clarify the meaning of the supplementary verses not recited by the ancient teachers, he says: "Of those employed by false disputants," and so forth. For "false disputants" refers to those who maintain the theory of counter-transformation (*pratirasapāka*), those who maintain the theory of the three types of transformation (*pākatraya*), those who maintain that the qualities (*guṇa*) are the agents of action, and others like them. "Refutation" (*pratiṣedhana*) is the criticism of the opposing position through the logical methods of the treatise (*tantrayukti*), such as *apadeśa* (citation of authority) and the rest. "Establishment of one's own statement" (*svavākyasiddhi*) is the defense of one's own position through the logical method of the treatise known as "determination" (*nirṇaya*).

Just as the view of those who propound that "digestion occurs according to each individual rasa" was refuted through the knowledge of substances and so forth by means of the *tantrayukti* called *apadeśa*, and the establishment of one's own position—that "digestion is of two kinds"—was accomplished in that very context by means of the *tantrayukti* called *nirṇaya*; likewise, those [topics] which were not explicitly stated (*vyakta*), meaning not clearly expressed; those which were hidden (*līna*), meaning not properly shown; and those which were impure (*anirmala*), meaning stated only in part—their thorough establishment is carried out by means of *yoga* and other such methods.
Just as the sun is for a lotus grove, or as a lamp is for a house...
Likewise, the logical arguments of the Tantra are for the purpose of illuminating awakening. ||7||

Some recite here a verse for the purpose of praising the *tantrayukti*s, beginning with "Just as the sun [is to] the lotus grove," and so forth. Yet this verse has not been cited as part of the root text in the commentaries. (7)
In that context, the subject matter with reference to which something is stated is the *adhikaraṇa* (topic); for example, "taste" or "defect. (8)

Hereafter, he provides an exposition of the aforementioned *tantrayukti*s (methodological principles of the treatise), beginning with the words "tatra" and so forth. In this context, "tatra" means among those *tantrayukti*s; that subject matter (*artha*) with reference to which other matters are expressed is known as *adhikaraṇa* (the governing topic). He gives an example: "rasaṃ doṣaṃ vā" (either *rasa* or *doṣa*). By this, the following is meant: whatever collection of meanings is expressed—even in the absence of an explicit mention of *rasa* or *doṣa*—all of that is understood to fall under that governing topic (*adhikāra*). ||8||
That by which a sentence is properly joined is *yoga*.
For example: "One should drink oil with *amṛtavallī*, *nimba*, *hiṃsrā*, *abhayā*, *vṛkṣaka*, and *pippalī*."

"In the case of 'siddhaṃ balābhyāṃ ca sadevadāru hitāya nityaṃ galagaṇḍaroge', although it should have been stated as 'pibet siddhaṃ tailam' (one should drink the prepared oil) at the beginning [of the third quarter], the word 'siddham' is employed in the third quarter; such unification of words situated even far apart is *yoga*. (9)

He states the *tantrayukti* called *yoga* with the words "by which," etc. The meaning is that *yoga* is the unification of words that have been stated out of order, whether they are proximate or remote. Demonstrating the application of words stated out of order, he says "oil," etc. The meaning is that *yoga* is the unification of a word that has been stated in reverse. The sūtra begins with "by which," etc.; the meaning of the sūtra is "by which [words] stated out of order," etc.; and "just as," etc., is the example.

Having thus established the primary unification (*ekīkaraṇa*) consisting in the removal of a proximate word that has been stated erroneously, he speaks by way of reference even to those [words] situated at a distance: "In this way, even for those situated at a distance" (sūtra 9).

That meaning which is expressed in a *sūtra* or in a word is the *padārtha*; the meaning of a single word, of two words, or of many words is the *padārtha*, and these *padārthas* are indeed immeasurable.

Just as when oleation, sudation, and collyrium are prescribed, the attainment of two or three purposes is observed, one should accept that purpose which is established by the context of what precedes and follows; for example, when it is said, "We shall explain the chapter on the origin of the Vedas," the intellect hesitates—wondering which Veda he will describe the origin of—since there are the Rigveda and the others.

Because of the usage of these two roots—*vid* in the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇa*) and *vidlṛ* in the sense of "acquisition" (*lābha*), both of which have multiple meanings—one understands by observing the preceding and following context that the speaker intends to set forth the origin of Āyurveda; such is the meaning of the word. ||10||

He states the *tantrayukti* known as *padārthābhidhā* (the naming of word-meanings) with the words "The meaning which has been stated," and so forth. Since that by which a meaning is reached (*padyate*) or understood is a "word" (*pada*), and because a *sūtra* is also a word, the meaning propounded within a *sūtra* is a *padārtha*. Having thus stated the definition of the *tantrayukti* called *padārthābhidhā*, he now, desiring to explain it, first states the compound of its constituent parts with the words "Of the word," and so forth.

Now, having determined [the categories] among many objects, he explains the multiplicity of objects in order to grasp specific objects, beginning with "innumerable" (*aparimitā*) and so forth. To the question "How? he says "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth.

In that context, when the word *sneha* (unctuousness) is mentioned, the inclusion of three meanings—quality (*guṇa*), affection (*prema*), and clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*)—is observed. Likewise, by the word *sveda* (perspiration), there is the inclusion of both types of heat: that with fire and that without fire. By the word *añjana* (collyrium), there is also the inclusion of both eye-salve and medicinal application. Among those possible referents, he specifies which one is to be understood, saying "the meaning therein," and so forth. The sense is that whichever meaning is established through the connection between the previously stated and the subsequently stated sentences is the one to be accepted.

He provides an example, beginning with "as in the case of the origin of the Veda" (*yathā vedotpattim*). "Is doubted" (*sandihyate*) means that one falls into doubt. He explains how it is doubted with the words "of which one? (*katamasya*), and so forth. Since there are the Vedas such as the *Ṛgveda* and others, one doubts: "Of which Veda will he speak regarding its origin? Regarding that doubt, he states how the meaning should be accepted according to the context, beginning with "the Veda" (*vid*), and so forth: "We desire the *Āyurveda* being taught here"—in this [sentence], the word *Āyurveda* is heard; therefore, the intention here is that the "Veda" refers to the *Āyurveda*. (10)
Whatever else has been stated that serves to establish another meaning is the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*).
For example: "Just as a lump of clay is moistened with water, so too is a wound moistened with black gram, milk, and the like. (11)

He states the definition of the method of reasoning based on the meaning of cause (hetvarthatantrayukti) with the words "whatever else," etc. He provides an example with the words "just as clay," etc. Here, by means of the external illustration of a lump of clay, the internal moistening of a wound is established through such things as the application of black gram and milk. ||11||
A brief statement is an enumeration (*uddeśa*); for example: "the arrow" (*śalyam*). ||12||

He states the definition of *uddeśa* (brief enunciation) with the words "in brief," and so forth. The meaning is that *uddeśa* is a statement made concisely. He provides an example with the words "just as a thorn. Everything that produces affliction is briefly called a "thorn" (*śalya*), and not because of a detailed elaboration based on the distinction between endogenous and exogenous types. ||12||
Detailed explanation is the exposition; for example: "bodily and adventitious. (13)

He states the definition of exposition (*nirdeśa*): "In detail," and so forth. The meaning is that exposition is speaking at length. He provides an example: "As internal and external," and so forth. A wound (*śalya*) is said to be of two kinds: the internal wound and the external wound. (13)
"Thus" refers to the instruction. As it is said: "One should not remain awake at night, and one should avoid sleeping during the day. (14)

He states the definition of instruction (*upadeśa*): "In this way," and so forth. The meaning is that instruction is that which says, "One should act in this manner. He provides an example: "For instance," and so forth. Now, one might ask: what is the difference between instruction (*upadeśa*) and a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*)? It is said in reply: instruction is generally applicable (*prāyika*), as for example, "One should not stay awake at night" is presented as a general rule, since staying awake at night is also recommended when one is overcome by phlegm (*kapha*) and the like. Likewise, "One should not sleep during the day" is also generally applicable, since sleeping during the day is appropriate in the summer or when afflicted by thirst and similar conditions. An injunction (*niyoga*), however, is not generally applicable.

For example: "One should eat only what is wholesome. Although there may be occasions for even unwholesome food, as in the statement, "A person with fever may eat what is unwholesome, even if he has no appetite," and so forth, nevertheless, at that time, it is precisely the unwholesome that possesses the nature of being wholesome; thus, there is no deviation from the injunction. ||14||
The term *apadeśa* refers to the statement of a reason; for example, as it is stated: "Sweet [substance] increases phlegm. (15)

He states the definition of *apadeśa* (the reason): "By this," and so forth. The meaning is that *apadeśa* is the statement of a cause with respect to an effect, in the form "by this [cause]. He provides an example: "As it is pointed out," and so forth. The phrase "as it is pointed out" introduces the example. [Question: Why does a specific substance that is sweet increase *śleṣman* (phlegm)? [Answer: Here, "sweet increases *śleṣman*" means that it increases it by its own nature, namely, by its sweetness. ||15||

Pradeśa (the illustration by reference) is the proof of a subject under discussion by means of what has already been established. For example: "Just as this [man] extracted the arrow from Devadatta, so too will he extract it from Yajñadatta. (16)

He states the scope: "of the subject at hand," and so forth. He provides an example: "as in the case of Devadatta," and so forth. Here, Yajñadatta’s extraction of a thorn is the topic under discussion, and that is established by means of Devadatta’s previously mentioned extraction of a thorn. ||16||
1. *Atideśa* (extended application) is the proof of what is not yet mentioned by means of what has been discussed.
For example: "Because his wind rises upward from this [condition], he would be one with upward-moving wind (*udāvartin*). ||17||

He states the extension [of a rule] with the words "of the subject matter," and so forth. "Of what has not yet come" means of what is yet to be. He provides an example with the words "just as from which," and so forth. Here, the upward movement of the wind (*vāyu*) is the subject matter under discussion. By means of that subject matter, the future state of being afflicted by *udāvarta* (upward-moving disorder) is established. "One would be afflicted by *udāvarta*" means that one might be expected to suffer from *udāvarta*. ||17|| Exclusion (*apavarga*) is the removal [of a term] after it has been pervaded [by a general rule]. For example: "Those [substances] contaminated by poison are not to be sweated, except for insect poisons. ||18||

He states *apavarga* (separation): "having pervaded," and so forth. (*Apavarga* is the separation of some object from its qualities, actions, and so on, after having been completely pervaded by those qualities, actions, and so on, from all sides). He provides an example: "such as those that should not be sweated," and so forth. Having established that those afflicted by poison should not be sweated by way of a general rule (*utsarga*), he states the exception (*apavāda*): "except in other cases," and so forth. ||18||

That word by which a sentence is completed when it has not been explicitly stated is called *vākyaśeṣa* (the remainder of the sentence). For example, when it is said, "of the head, hands, feet, sides, back, belly, and chest," even without the mention of "man," it is understood that [these belong] to a man. ||19||
He states the remainder of the sentence with "by which," etc. He provides an illustration with "just as the head," etc. The meaning is that it is understood, i.e., known. ||19||
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is that which is understood by implication from what has been stated.
For example, when it is said, "I shall eat rice," it is understood by implication that this person is not thirsty and does not [wish to drink] barley-gruel. (20)

He states the presumption (*arthāpatti*) with the words "that which is not mentioned," and so forth. Regarding that which is not mentioned—that is, not explicitly stated—he provides an example with the words "just as rice," and so forth; the meaning is that this person does not wish to drink the gruel. ||20||
The opposite of what is stated here is its reversal (*viparyaya*).
For example, when it is said that those who are emaciated, weak, or timid are difficult to treat, the opposite is understood: those who are robust and so forth are easy to treat. (21)

He states the opposite [case] with the words "If that which was stated here," and so forth. *Prātilomya* means the reverse. He provides an example with the words "As in the case of 'emaciated and slight,'" and so forth. In the case of the opposite, the contrary itself is understood; however, in the case of *arthāpatti*, the non-contrary meaning alone is cognized through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). This is the distinction between the two. ||21||

*Prasaṅga* (incidental discussion) is the conclusion by means of another context; or rather, that matter which was stated more than once and interrupted by another context is concluded—that is *prasaṅga*. For example: after stating in the *Vedotpatti* [chapter] that "the person (*puruṣa*) is a composite of the five great elements and the embodied soul; activity resides in him, and he is the substratum," it is stated again during the investigation of the elements: "Since it has been declared that the person is a composite of the five great elements and the embodied soul, this very person, as the subject of action, is the one qualified for medical treatment. (22)

He states the consequence: "by means of another context," and so forth. "By means of another context" means by means of a matter stated in another context. "Equal" means identical. He provides an example: "as," and so forth. "Repeatedly stated in other contexts" means stated again and again. "Is concluded" means it is brought to completion. That very point is explained: "as," and so forth.

Others, however, read "an artha that has been stated more than once, separated by another section" and explain it as follows: a person with acute fever (navajvarin) is prohibited [from oleation] in the sections on oleation (sneha) and purgation (vireka); then, in the section on fever, the oleation and purification of one with fresh fever are again prohibited. Thus, there is a repeated statement of a matter that was separated by an intervening section. ||22||
(Throughout) that which is expressed with a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is "exclusive" (*ekānta*). For example: "The *trivṛt* purges [only]," or "the *madanaphala* emetics [only]. ||23||

He states the definition of exclusivity (*ekānta-lakṣaṇa*) with the words "in all cases" (*sarvatra*), etc. By the term "restriction" (*avadhāraṇa*), he means "without exception" (*avikalpena*), that is to say, "necessarily. He provides an example, since the particle *eva*, which expresses restriction, is indicated in the illustration: "Just as the threefold [mixture] purges" (*yathā trivṛd virecayati*). ||23||
That which is "thus in some cases and otherwise in others" is non-absolutism (anekānta).
For example—some teachers say that substance (*dravya*) is primary, some say taste (*rasa*), some say potency (*vīrya*), and some say post-digestive effect (*vipāka*). 24.

He states the non-absolutist position (anekānta) with the words "in some cases it is so," and so forth. He provides an illustration: "For example, some teachers say that substance (dravya) is primary," and so on. The meaning is clear. ||24||
A preliminary objection is a question preceded by an objection; for example: "How is it that the four types of urinary disorders caused by wind (vāta) become incurable? ||25||

He states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Objection" (*ākṣepa*), etc. He provides an example with the words "For instance" (*yathā*), etc. Here, the introduction of the prima facie position is due to the reason that the various defects are perceived as being the very things to be proven (*sādhya*). Even doubt (*saṃśaya*) possesses the capacity to establish the object, insofar as it serves as a constituent part of the final determination (*nirṇaya*). ||25||

The resolution to that [objection] is as follows: Just as the wind, having compressed the body and subsequently moved downward, discharges urine permeated by fat, marrow, and muscle-fat, so too are those born of Vāta incurable. ||26||
And so it has been said: "When the wind, joined with fat, marrow, and grease, compresses the entire body and becomes aggravated below, those diseases born of wind (vāta) are incurable. (27)

He states the conclusion: "The answer to that," and so forth. The meaning is that the answer to that prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is the conclusion (nirṇaya). He provides an example: "As for the body," and so forth. Since the wind (vāta), having caused affliction to the body and so on, discharges urine accompanied by fat and other tissues, therefore, upon the depletion of the marrow (majjan), there is incurability due to the sequential depletion of the preceding elements (dhātus); this is the meaning. ||26-27||
An opponent's view that is not refuted is accepted.
For example, if another were to say, "There are seven tastes," that is accepted in some sense because it is not refuted. ||28||

He states what is agreed upon: "the opinion of another," and so forth. This means that which is not refuted is accepted. He provides an example: "just as," and so forth. "In some way" means by some manner whatsoever. ||28||
The procedure has been stated according to the sequence of the chapters; for example—the eleven vital points (marmans) of the thighs have been stated according to the sequence of the chapters. ||29||

He states the definition: "The sequence of topics," and so forth. This means it is stated according to the order of the sections. Candranandana has defined the characteristic of *vidhāna* as "the exposition of the subject matter in its proper sequence. He provides an example: "As for the thighs," and so forth. The statement of the vital points (*marmans*) according to the sequence of their respective sections begins with "the insteps, the soles, the heart," and so on. ||29||
"Thus he will say" refers to looking toward the future; for example, as one might say in the *Ślokasthāna*: "I shall explain [this] in the *Cikitsitasthāna*. (30)

He speaks of "looking toward the future" with the words "In this way," and so forth. This means the observation of what is yet to come—that which will be—out of regard for the purpose of the task at hand. He provides an illustration with the words "Just as in the verse," and so forth. ||30||

That which was stated previously is "oversight of what has passed. For example, in the section on therapeutics (cikitsita), one might say: "as it was declared in the Section on General Principles (ślokasthāna). ||31||

He speaks of "reviewing what has passed" (*atikrāntāvekṣaṇa*) with the words beginning "that which," and so forth. Reviewing what has passed means looking back at what is past. He provides an illustration with the words beginning "just as in medical treatments," and so forth. ||31||
Doubt arises from the perception of two opposing causes; for example: "A blow to the chest is fatal, whereas the severing of hands and feet is not fatal. (32)

He states the doubt with the words "ubhaya" and so forth. It is the perception of the cause of two dissimilar objects. He provides an example with the words "yathā tala" and so forth. [Objection: But this was cited for the purpose of illustrating doubtful cognition; from where does the doubt arise? For the striking of the palm against the heart and the cutting off of the hand and so forth have been shown separately by virtue of being life-threatening and not life-threatening. [Response: True; however, where both striking and cutting exist, there arises a doubt as to whether death results from the striking of the palm against the heart, or whether survival results from the cutting off of the hands and feet. ||32||
An exposition (*vyākhyāna*) is the description of a specific excellence within a treatise (*tantra*).
For example: "Here, the twenty-fifth principle, the *puruṣa*, is explained; whereas in other medical treatises (*āyurvedatantra*), the analysis begins with the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth. (33)

He states the definition: "In the *tantra*, etc. *Tantra* means a treatise (*śāstra*). An exposition (*vyākhyāna*) is the description or manifestation of an excellence (*atiśaya*), that is, an additional meaning. Regarding the reading "an excellence therein" (*tatrātiśaya*), the word "therein" (*tatra*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). He provides an example: "As here, etc. The term "the twenty-fifth person" (*pañcaviṃśatikaḥ puruṣaḥ*) means the twenty-fifth; for there are twenty-four principles consisting of the eight [beginning with] the unmanifest (*avyakta*), together with the sixteen transformations of nature (*prakṛti-vikāra*). "Person" (*puruṣa*) refers to the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

Having stated his own view, he states the view of others, beginning with the words "In other Ayurvedic treatises," and so forth. "The Bhūtādi [tanmātra] is the tāmasa ahaṃkāra"; by this it is meant that in other Ayurvedic treatises, the analysis begins from the Bhūtādi ahaṃkāra, and not from the avyakta (the unmanifest). ||33||
A technical term not shared with other treatises;
for example, "mithuna" as a designation for honey and clarified butter, or an illustration well-known in common usage. ||34||

He states his own technical terminology (*svasañjñā*): "Technical terminology not common to other treatises," and so forth. Other treatises are those other than Āyurveda, such as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and others; "not common" means unique, that is to say, not followed therein [in those other sciences], but rather useful only within one's own treatises. He provides an example: "For instance, *mithuna*," and so forth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the application of one's own technical term (*svasañjñā*) is made for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), and yet here no such usage is observed by means of the term "pair" (*mithuna*) through which honey and ghee are taken? [Reply: It is said: this is merely an example, given in whatever way possible. For this very reason, he states another alternative: "Or an example well-known in the world. This means that it should be understood as a technical term (*svasañjñā*), just as the term "great unctuous substance" (*mahāsneha*) is applied to four types of unctuous substances.

Beyond this, some read as follows: "Just as one pursues shade out of fear of heat. They, however, consider this even to be an *udāharaṇa* (illustration) among the *tantrayukti*s (methodological principles). That is not correct, because the *tantrayukti* called *udāharaṇa* is not mentioned in the *uddeśa-sūtra* (the sūtra of enumeration), and because it would result in an excess in the number [of *tantrayukti*s]. Therefore, the passage beginning with "just as one [fears] heat" is simply a corrupt reading. ||34||
A definitive statement is a *nirvacana* (etymological derivation).
For example: "Ayurveda" [is so called] because life (*āyus*) exists in it, or by means of it, or because one attains life through it. 35.
He states the etymological derivation: "ascertained," and so forth. He provides an illustration: "as in 'life exists in this,'" and so forth. ||35||

An illustration (*nidarśana*) is the manifestation of an example (*dṛṣṭāntavyakti*). For instance: "Just as fire, when accompanied by wind, increases in dry grass (*kakṣa*), so too does a wound increase when the wind, bile, and phlegm are deranged. (36)

He states the definition of *nidarśana* (illustration): "The manifestation by means of an example," and so forth. A sentence in which there is manifestation (*vyakti*) by means of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is thus [defined]. By this, the following is meant: that in which the matter is established by means of an example is an illustration. For this very reason, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is distinct from the illustration, because the meaning of the reason consists merely of the example itself. He provides an example: "Just as fire," and so forth. The word "thus" (*tathā*) means that it undergoes increase. ||36||

"Only this should be done" is an injunction (*niyoga*). For example: "One should eat only what is wholesome. [The author] states the injunction with the words "only this," etc., and provides an illustration with the words "for example, what is wholesome," etc. [Objection: In some cases, an injunction is transgressed; for instance, when a fever patient has a loss of appetite, even unwholesome food is given. As it is said: "If a fever patient should have a loss of appetite, he may eat what is unwholesome; for by not eating at the time of meals, he either wastes away or dies."
It is also stated in another Tantra: "Indeed, that state arises in relation to place, time, and strength, in which what is a duty becomes a non-duty, and even what is forbidden becomes a duty. (37)
"Both this and that" refers to a collective grouping (*samuccaya*).
For example: "In the category of meat, the black antelope, the deer, and so forth, as well as the common quail, the partridge, and the francolin, are the principal [kinds]. (38)

He states the conjunction (*samuccaya*) with "this" and so forth. He gives an example with "as meat" and so forth; for instance, "the *eṇa* deer and others are primary [meats], and the *lāva* birds and others are also primary"—this is conjunction (*samuccaya*). (38) The alternative (*vikalpa*) is expressed as "this or that. For example: "Let there be either rice with sauce or barley gruel with ghee. (39)

He states the alternative (*vikalpa*): "This or that," and so forth. The reason why the word *vā* (or) is not employed for each individual example here is to show that even with a single *vā*, the state of being an alternative (*vikalpatā*) is seen among many options. Sometimes an alternative occurs even without the word *vā*, as when regarding a single disease there are many formulations (*yoga*); even without the word *vā*, one of the formulations is to be applied—this is an alternative. He gives an example: "such as rice with sauce," and so forth. 39.

That which is not explicitly stated but is understood through intelligence is to be inferred (*ūhya*). For example, in the section on the rules for food and drink (*annapānavidhi*), four types of food are taught—namely, that which is to be chewed (*bhakṣya*), that which is to be eaten (*bhojya*), that which is to be licked (*lehya*), and that which is to be drunk (*peya*)—yet when four types ought to have been mentioned, only two are stated. Here, this must be inferred: by mentioning two specific categories among food and drink, all four are effectively included. Furthermore, a fourfold diet is rare; generally, it is only twofold. Therefore, duality is well-established.

Furthermore: by means of solid food (*anna*), that which is to be chewed (*bhakṣya*) is encompassed, due to the common property of solidity; by means of that which is to be drunk (*peya*), that which is to be licked (*lehya*) is encompassed, due to the common property of fluidity. ||40||

Now he states the *tantrayukti* called "inference" (*ūhya*), beginning with the words "that which... and so forth. "Unspecified" means not explicitly stated. He provides an example, beginning with "as has been stated," and so forth. To explain how something becomes inferable here, he says: "While it should have been stated as fourfold—namely, that which is to be chewed (*bhakṣya*), that which is to be swallowed (*bhojya*), that which is to be licked (*lehya*), and that which is to be drunk (*peya*)—only two types were mentioned; thus, the fourfold nature remains to be inferred. Regarding what kind of intellect perceives this "inferable" (*ūhya*) which was previously established as being accessible to the intellect, he says: "In food and drink," and so forth.

By the mention of "food and drink" (*annapāna*) as specific types of edibles (*abhyavahārya*), there is the inclusion of the four specific categories of edibles: *bhakṣya* (chewable), *bhojya* (masticable), *lehya* (lickable), and *peya* (drinkable). Anticipating the objection—"Why was this fourfold nature not stated directly?"—he says: "It is fourfold," and so forth. "Scanty" (*pravirala*) means excessively sparse, because it exists only occasionally and in some way or another. He states the fourfold nature by yet another method: "Furthermore, moreover," and so forth.

Regarding this, some raise an objection: since the meaning of a sentence that is unclear or not explicitly present is to be inferred through interpretation (*yojanā*), it is "to be inferred" (*ūhya*) and not a "tantra-method" (*tantrayukti*). However, because an implied (*līna*) or unstated (*anirdiṣṭa*) meaning—whether of both types—is inferred from the sentence itself and then interpreted, it is indeed a "tantra-method. (40)
And there are verses on this point:
"The systematic arrangement of these [faculties] has been demonstrated by way of their general characteristics;
however, the specific details should be discerned by the wise according to their application. (41)
Indeed, these thirty-two methods, endowed with word, meaning, and logic, have been properly set forth by me for the sake of seeking the essence of the Tantra. (42)
For that wise physician who knows the *Ottara* according to the rules and has become like a lamp is worthy of worship; this is the opinion of Dhanvantari. (43)

Having thus stated the *tantrayukti*s (methodological principles of the treatise), he concludes by reciting a verse—beginning with "And there are here..."—in order to facilitate the understanding of the specific *tantrayukti*s that have been explained. The meaning is that the specific application of these *tantrayukti*s should be grasped by the learned according to their respective contexts. Kārtika, however, recites two verses beginning with "The thirty-two *yukti*s... [41–43].

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter (the third from the beginning), titled "The Methodological Arrangements of the Treatise" (*tantrayukti*), within the chapters on the ornaments of the treatise in the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter in the Uttaratantra of the commentary on the Suśruta Saṃhitā, titled Nibandhasaṅgraha, composed by the illustrious Ḍalhaṇa.
The method of the treatise consists of: the subject matter, the connection, the purpose, the meaning of the words,
the reference, the enumeration, the detailed explanation, the supplementary statement, and the motive.
Instruction, indirect instruction, extension, presumption, and determination;
the ancillaries, the certain, the uncertain, and error with its sub-divisions.
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), the injunction (vidhi), the consent (anumata), the exposition (vyākhyāna), and doubt (saṃśaya);
likewise, reference to the past and future, one's own technical term (svasaṃjñā), and non-aggregation (asamuccaya).

Illustration (*nidarśana*), etymological derivation (*nirvacana*), application (*niyoga*), alternative interpretation (*vikalpana*), rebuttal (*pratyutsāra*), extraction (*uddhāra*), and possibility (*sambhava*) are the *tantra-yuktis* (methodologies of the system). The term "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth refers to these methodologies. A *yukti* is the joining together of the meanings of sentences; it is that by means of which, without such joinings, the system (*tantra*) would remain unconnected. What are these methodologies? In this context, "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*). *Adhikaraṇa* means introduction (*prastāva*). Even when a collection of meanings has been stated elsewhere, that by whose force it is established in its specific place is the *adhikaraṇa*.
Just as some say "seven days" while others say "ten days," the general meaning of the statement is established in the specific case called fever by virtue of the context. ||1||

What is called *yoga* is connection (*sambandha*), and that [connection] exists either between word-meanings (*padārtha*) or between sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*). Among these, the connection between word-meanings occurs by way of the relationship of the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhakabhāva*). For example, in the passage beginning with "the diseases such as passion," there is a connection between the word-meaning "together with their roots" (*samūlāḥ*) and the word-meaning "cast away" (*apāstāḥ*). As for the connection between sentence-meanings, it is as follows: when there is doubt regarding what has been digested and what has not, one should drink hot water again; by that, there shall be purification of eructation, and from that, lightness and relish [of food]. ||2||

The meaning of "the cause" (hetvartha) is that which, when stated in one place, is likewise applicable elsewhere. For example, by the statement "there, in each individual branch," it is understood that the remaining branches are also to be known. ||3||
A "word-meaning" (padārtha) is that meaning which is understood from a word; for example, qualities such as "heavy" and so forth are understood from words denoting qualities. 4.

A "pradeśa" (extended application) is that where, by virtue of the statement regarding one part of a subject matter, the remainder of it is understood even though it is not explicitly stated. For example, when cakes are described as having an extreme lightness resulting from the process of baking in chaff and so forth, by virtue of that description, other prepared foods which are not mentioned are likewise understood to be so. ||5||

Specification (nirdeśa) is the reiteration of those things already indicated by their mere names, for the purpose of demonstrating their specific nature; for example, having first mentioned "hurriedly raised" and so forth in the context of a calamity to property, the phrase "but bound without breathing" is stated in order to demonstrate the defects among them. ||7||

The "remainder of the sentence" (vākyaśeṣa) refers to that part of a sentence which remains [unspoken] when only a portion is stated; although not explicitly uttered at the time of explanation, it follows by implication. For example, in the statement, "Disease is the imbalance of the humors (doṣa), while health is the equilibrium of the humors," the phrase "it is said" (ucyate) is the remainder of the sentence. Thus, in the case of "Disease is the imbalance of the humors, while health is the equilibrium of the humors," the phrase "it is said" constitutes the remainder of the sentence. ||8||

The "purpose" (prayojana) is that which one undertakes to accomplish for which an action is begun; for example, the drinking of medicine is undertaken to accomplish the digestion of the remainder of the humors and the kindling of the digestive fire in those who have morbid humors. (9)

Instruction (upadeśa) is the proclamation of the pure word of a reliable authority; for example: "The embryo faces the mother's back, with palms joined at the forehead and limbs contracted," and so forth. 10.

"Statement" (apadeśa) means: the statement of the reason for proving that which has been asserted as a pure word of authority. For example, in the proposition "successively more harmful are the corrupted wind and other humors," the reason is "because they are difficult to ward off. ||11||
Extension (atideśa) is the application of properties belonging to one thing to another; for example, the application of properties belonging to *pālakyā* to *cuccū*. 12.

Presumption (arthāpatti) is that wherein, when one matter is being stated, another matter not explicitly mentioned is necessarily implied by the force [of the context]; that is presumption. For example, when it is said regarding water that has been boiled, "Even though it is old, raw [water] must not be drunk," the [word] "because of not eating" is understood through the power of the sense, even though it is not explicitly stated. 13.

Conclusion (*nirṇaya*) is the rendering of the stated topics free from expectancy by means of what has not been explicitly stated; for example, the rendering of the diseases mentioned in the "Knowledge of Diseases of the Eyelids" free from expectancy through the "Therapeutics of Diseases of the Eyelids. (14)

Prasaṅga (incidental mention) is the mention of even a topic that is not under discussion by virtue of some connection; for that indeed is prasaṅga. For example, in the context of vomiting, the mention of "generally by all [medicines] ending with smoke" and so forth, which is not part of the current subject matter. 15.

"Exclusivity" (ekānta) means that which excludes other alternatives; that is exclusivity. For example, because it is stated that [suffering] is produced from the causes of defects, its being "intrinsic" (nijatva) is never produced by external causes; that is exclusivity. Just as the statement that it is produced from the causes of defects does not encompass its being intrinsic as something never produced by external causes. (16)

That which, even when stated, is not certain by virtue of its being inevitable is called "non-absolute" (anaikānta). For example, the statement, "A fever that has arisen will subside after six nights," though so stated, is non-absolute because it is not necessarily inevitable. ||17||

Apavarga (exclusion) is the drawing out by means of a specific term of that which has entered into a general statement; it is "with exclusion" (sopavarga). For example, when it is said that "sweet things are phlegm-generating," this applies to things like old rice that have entered [into the category]; [apavarga] is the drawing out of these by means of a word. 18.

Contrariety (viparyaya) means the state of being otherwise than what was stated; contrariety is the opposite of what was described regarding the etiology, such as when there is no relief from those factors that cause the disease, while there is relief from their opposites. ||19||

The prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is a collection of statements intended to demonstrate the untenability of the opponent's thesis; for example, the statements establishing that there are many tastes directed against one who maintains that there are only six tastes. 20.

*Vidhāna* refers to the arrangement made by the author of the tantra; it is the specific composition of words and so forth. For example, with the intention that there should be no cessation of worldly practice due to a thorough knowledge of all contradictions, it was stated: "And that knowledge is not exclusively auspicious. (21)

"Consent" (anumata) means the acceptance even of a divergent opposing position; for example, when prescribing an enema (vasti), the acceptance that all this should be validated by means of reasoning, opinion, defects, medicine, strength, and so forth. ||22||

"Exposition" (vyākhyāna) means the detailed explanation of a meaning that has been stated briefly; or else, it is that which was not explicitly expressed [in the root text] but has come down through the succession of the lineage of gurus, explained by means of clear words. (23)
Doubt (saṃśaya) is the lack of certainty regarding contradictory positions; for example, as in the case of various possibilities arising from the onset of poison. (24)

"Dependence on the past" (atītāpekṣā) refers to that case where a connection with meaning arises by depending upon a preceding word. For example, when it is said, "Those who are to be sweated and so forth are those to be oleated," one expects [the qualification] "but not those with extremely weak digestion" for the term "those to be oleated. And as in the case of the statement in the aphorism, "One should perform fasting during fever," one expects the specific fasting mentioned in the rule. ||25||

"Expectation of what follows" (anāgatāpekṣā) refers to that case where, depending upon a subsequent word, there arises the sense of a connection; this is "expectation of what follows. For example, in the description of the daily regimen (*dinacaryā*), such as "thereafter, [the administration of] nasal drops, gargles, and so forth," the procedures for nasal therapy and the like are expected. ||26||
A "technical term" (svasaṃjñā) is that which is heard only in its own [specific] treatise and not in another; for example, *āpāna* for *jentāka*, and so forth. 27.

That which is called "to be inferred" (ūhya) is that which, although not explicitly stated by the word, is established through the physician's own wisdom; for example, [the rule] "one should abandon a substance that is non-etymological"—that which is non-etymological is established by wisdom even though it was not mentioned by the word. ||28||

Combination (*samuccaya*) means that when one [treatment] has been prescribed, the prescription of a second [treatment] for that same condition without contradicting the former; for example, for wind (*vāta*), oleation (*sneha*), sudation (*sveda*), and so forth. 29.

Illustration (nidarśana) is defined as an example that constitutes a part of the thesis to be proven; for instance, regarding the three types of disorders caused by undigested matter (āmadoṣa), fasting, digestive treatments, and purification therapies serve as the illustration. This applies to such statements as: "In the same manner, one should treat other diseases by means of measures contrary to their respective etiological factors. (30)

Etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is the application of a name as it was stated by convention to its actual meaning; for example, "cholera" (*viṣūcikā*) because it pierces the limbs as if with needles. (31)
"Niyojana" (command) refers to the application of actions or operations; for example: "Even though you are overcome by perspiration and fainting, this ball must not be released by you. (32)
Vikalpa (alternation) is the mention of possible alternatives either successively or simultaneously; for example: "One should perform fasting during the onset of fever and so forth. (33)

*Pratyutsāra* is that wherein, while demonstrating their own positions, they refute one another's views. For example: "A pregnant woman in the eighth month should drink milk-gruel mixed with ghee," says Khaṇḍakāpya; "No," says Bhagavān Ātreya, "for fear of harming the fetus by causing jaundice (*paiṅgalya*). "Let there be the risk of jaundice," [replies the former], "but even so, by acting thus, she gives birth to a child free from disease and endowed with strength, complexion, and other qualities. (34)

"Exposition" (uddhāra) refers to the resolution of an objection raised in a treatise. For example, when a teacher has stated, "The enema is produced by the qualities of painting," and so forth, up to the objection, "How does it remove the humors from all sides?", the resolution is, "This [enema] is subject to the stagnant wind," and so forth. (35)

Sambhava (logical possibility) is that by which something is established through a rule that is not observed elsewhere; it is "sambhava" because it is established by such a rule. For example, when causes, symptoms, and medicines for all diseases are stated in general terms, the establishment of specific details such as [the predominance of] Vāta and so forth is obtained through the grace of sambhava. Thus are the *tantrayukti*s (methodological principles).

Although, according to the system of the Bhaṭṭāraka, there remain four [types of questions]: those requiring a categorical answer, those requiring a counter-question, those requiring a rejection, and those requiring an explanation of the reason, nevertheless, because they are not formally integrated into this Tantra by the Teacher, they are not mentioned here. Alternatively, their status as "Tantra-yukti" (structural principles of the treatise) is simply not accepted. Furthermore, regarding the statement on the excessive application of fire (*agnyatiyoga*), the determination of its specific variations according to the particular humors (*vāta*, etc. is indeed obtainable through the grace of what is possible; thus, it has been stated.
Just as the rays of the sun [awaken] a lake of sleeping lotuses,
and just as the light of lamps [illuminates] a house, so do the principles of the system [illuminate] the treatise.
Even while studying the treatises, one who is unskilled in the principles of methodology does not comprehend the meaning of the treatise,
just as one fails to obtain wealth when fortune has exhausted.

The passage beginning with "sarasa" and so forth is easy to understand. One who is unskilled in the principles of the treatise (*tantrayukti*)—that is, one who is incapable regarding these thirty-six principles of the treatise—does not comprehend, nor does he attain, the meaning of the treatise, just as one cannot obtain wealth when fortune has been exhausted.

These arguments, through their application to the meaning of the sentences, grant the attainment of the desired goal and serve as refutations of the statements employed by proponents of false doctrines.
They are the illuminators of those [meanings] expressed through ellipsis, transposition, and subtle nuances;
having thus grasped the essence of the ocean of the logic of sentences, they have established themselves in this way.

These logical methods (yukti) grant the accomplishment of one's own desired [conclusion] by virtue of joining together the meaning of a sentence; they are the refuters of those statements of false disputants which aim to demonstrate a connection of meanings that does not exist; and they are the revealers of what is stated cryptically (līna) and what is stated in inverted order (vyatyāsa). That which cannot be clearly expressed is "cryptic" (līna). "Inverted order" (vyatyāsa) is mutual transposition. "Hint" (leśa) is contact by way of a partial aspect. "Statement" (ukti) is a particular turn of speech.

These logical methods, which arise in innumerable ways from the ocean of the principles of sentence-structure, have been established here by extracting only their essence, much like the *jātis* of music extracted from song. As for the application of word-meanings, however, these are already well-known to those who are learned; therefore, they were not stated by the Teacher.

The word *yukti* (reasoning) indeed signifies a means (*upāya*). For it is not possible to compose a treatise (*tantra*) while rejecting these reasonings. Among them, some reasonings serve the purpose of the expression, such as enumeration (*uddeśa*), definition (*nirdeśa*), and so forth; others serve the purpose of the meaning, such as the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*), the categories (*padārtha*), and so forth. In this context, "subject matter" (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to that with reference to which a scripture proceeds—whether it be a section (*sthāna*), a chapter (*adhyāya*), a topic (*prakaraṇa*), or a sentence (*vākya*). Among these, the subject matter of the entire treatise is that with reference to which the treatise as a whole proceeds.

Just as the entire treatise known as the *Hṛdaya* proceeds by taking the eight branches [of medicine] as its subject matter—as stated in the passage beginning with "the body, pediatrics," and so forth—so too does the section on locations (*sthāna*) proceed, as in the passage beginning with "herein, the subtle points summarized [in the aphorisms] are now expanded upon. This should be understood to apply to the chapters (*adhyāya*) and other divisions as well.

*Yoga* means connection (*yojanā*), specifically the connection between a brief statement (*uddeśa*) and its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*), or between a sūtra and its commentary (*bhāṣya*). Alternatively, *yoga* is reasoning (*yukti*), which is fivefold: proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*). For instance: "Fire is the root of the body" is the proposition. "Because when food is digested by it, the body persists" is the reason. This is supported by the statement: "For from food, the unripened [nutrients] such as *rasa* do not arise."

The example is: "just as the seed is [the cause] of the rice sprout. The application (*upanaya*) consists of the various examples provided by the author of the treatise (*tantrakṛt*) to establish that the science of medicine possesses a purpose, such as: "for whom are fire, water, and so forth not established? Therefore, the application is: "the science of medicine indeed possesses a purpose, because its results are directly perceptible."

Therefore, the conclusion is presented by way of demonstrating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), stating that [the procedure] must be undertaken. As it was stated regarding medical treatment—beginning with "endowed with the four components and the qualities"—the application of the means of valid cognition and its result is established through the demonstration that doubt is untenable.

The meaning of the reason (*hetu*) mentioned in another context applies here as well, as in the passage beginning "therefore, in each individual branch," and likewise in "those not to be pierced are those that are conjoined or knotted," and so forth. From these specific statements, it is inferred that the remaining ones are to be pierced; otherwise, these words would be meaningless.

*Padārtha* (the meaning of a word) refers to that which is understood from a word; for example, the word "substance" (*dravya*) has earth, water, and so forth as its meaning, while the word "quality" (*guṇa*) has heaviness and so forth as its meaning.

*Pradeśa* (a partial indication) refers to those objects which, due to their extreme abundance, cannot be expressed in their entirety, and thus only a small portion is mentioned, such as when it is said, "a part of substance," and so on.
*Uddeśa* (an enumeration) refers to a concise statement, such as "wind" and "bile," which is a summary of the *doṣas*.

* Nirdeśa (explanation) is the detailed exposition of that very [subject], as stated there: "rough, light," and so forth. * Vākyaśeṣa (complementary statement) is that which, in a given aphorism, is supplied for the sake of completion because it is understood through the sense, though not explicitly stated; for example, in that context, "cavities arise in this body"—this is the complementary statement—because the suffix is used in the sense of "originating therein" in the subsequent passage, "the tongue is watery due to the moisture of taste. * Prayojana (purpose) is that for the sake of which a treatise or similar work is undertaken; for example, "the physician’s remedy is a hand-hold for those sunk in the mire of disease."
Instruction (*upadeśa*) is the word of a reliable authority (*āpta*), such as: "The internal cavities are moistened by unctuous substances," and so forth.

Explanation (*apadeśa*) is when a teacher, having proposed a certain matter, teaches the reason for it; for example, the proposition: "The life of all who are dying is not due to medicine"; he states the reason: "For not all diseases depend upon a remedy."

*Atideśa* (extended application) means teaching by means of what has already been stated; it is an *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) that indicates that after stating some particular matter, one should understand that other [similar] things are to be understood in the same way for the sake of establishing unstated meanings. For example: "From the wood of the great *pañcamūla*, [an object] wrapped in linen [is made]. And likewise: "In the same way, [wood] from *bhadrakāṣṭha* and so forth should be employed," and so on.

*Arthāpatti* (presumption) is that by which, when a certain meaning has been stated, another meaning is understood as if it were explicitly spoken. For example: "He does not eat at night, nor is he hot [from fever]. It is not, however, stated that "he should eat during the day. This is understood through *arthāpatti*.

*Nirṇaya* (ascertainment) is the establishment of a matter that was previously undetermined. For example, after raising a doubt regarding the science of medicine with the words "O Blessed One, some are seen... and so forth, the subsequent reply for the sake of ascertainment begins with "In this way, medical treatment cannot possibly be the same," and so on.

Prasaṅga (incidental discussion) is the restatement of a previously mentioned subject through another connection. For example, in the section on venesection: having stated that blood is the origin of the body and that the body's maintenance occurs by means of it, the topic of the body (*śārīra*) is then discussed in the context of pure menstrual flow (*śuddhārtava*). This is not the fault of redundancy, because in the section on venesection, it was only stated that blood originates from the body, but its sequential order was not described;
whereas in the *Śārīra-sthāna*, the cause of the body is explained in detail according to its proper sequence.

"Certainty" (*ekānta*) means that which relies exclusively and without deviation upon one side alone, and not the other. For example: "Those [qualities] which arise from the elements," and so forth, meaning they are adventitious (*āgantuka*) rather than arising from the elements themselves.
"Uncertainty" (*anaikānta*) means the non-determination of either side. For example: "The life of all those who are dying is [sustained] by medicine and so forth."

*Apavarga* (exception) refers to the removal of a specific portion of that which has been prescribed in its entirety. For example, beginning with the statement, "One who has been treated with cold, hot, unctuous, dry, and other [therapies]... and having stated the general rule (*utsarga*)—"one should venesect the vein when blood is excessive and painful in order to drain it"—the author then states the exception regarding a specific part with the words, "but not less than sixteen [digits]," and so forth.

*Viparyaya* (contrariety) refers to performing the characteristics and so on in a manner contrary to what was taught. For example, after stating the characteristics of one properly unctuated as "favorability of *vāta*," etc., he states that the opposite occurs in the case of one who is dry (*rūkṣa*).

An *pūrvapakṣa* (prior position) is a statement that seeks to refute the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). For example, one desiring to explain what is beneficial and what is harmful says: "O Blessed One, as some are seen... and so forth, up to "...therefore, the result of the distinction between the beneficial and the harmful is uncertain.
A *vidhāna* (prescription) is that which they call a prescription according to the sequence of the context.

An *anumata* (consent) is, for instance, when others state that potency (*vīrya*) is of two kinds—hot and cold—and further say, "it is also of various natures," and so on; thus it is consented to and not a source of contradiction.

Explanation (*vyākhyāna*) refers to that which is accessible only to those with a superior intellect, such as the statement, "The *kalala* [embryonic stage] shall form after seven days," and so forth; for the states of this embryo cannot be known except through the vision of yoga (*yogadṛṣṭi*).
Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is the cognition of an uncertain object characterized by expectancy, such as, "He who considers life to belong to one who has merely fallen into doubt," and so forth.

*Atītāvekṣaṇa* (retrospective reference) is that wherein the preparation of the subject at hand is explained by referring to what has already passed; for example, in the passage beginning with "rāsnā, jīvaka," etc., it says, "one should cook the great unctuous substance (*mahāsneha*). In this case, it is not known which specific *mahāsneha* is intended, and thus it is explained by referring back [to previous definitions]. *Anāgatāvekṣaṇa* (prospective reference) is that wherein a prior matter is established by referring to a procedure yet to come; for example, "one should employ emetics as prescribed in the section on wines (*madya-kalpa*)."

*Svasaṃjñā* (proprietary terminology) refers to terms coined by the authors of tantras for the sake of their own specific technical usage; it is not employed in other systems and is thus restricted [to them]. An example is: "the branches, the blood, etc., and the skin. *Ūhya* (that which is to be inferred) refers to that which is not explicitly recorded in this treatise, such as: "one should apply those groups according to the availability of the substances," and so forth. *Samuccaya* (combination) refers to that which combines items, such as when one combines *peyā* (gruel), *vilepī* (thick porridge), and both the unprepared and prepared forms.

Illustration (*nidarśana*) is that which is to be illustrated; it clarifies even a subtle matter through its own partial similarity, like a face in a mirror—for example, water and the like colored by safflower and so forth. Etymology (*nirvacana*) is a derivative explanation (*nirukta*); for example, "the world" (*jagat*) because it moves (*gacchati*), or "poison" (*viṣa*) because it causes trembling (*vepate*), and so forth. Prescription (*niyoga*) is a diverse determination, such as "this must be done" or "that must be done"; for example, light food or fasting in cases of fever and the like during its initial stages.

*Pratyutsāra* (counter-removal) is that wherein, while demonstrating the basis for their own position, they refute the opinions of others. For example, in the passage beginning "six hundred bones," etc., one refutes the previous opinion by establishing two thousand joints, thereby removing sixty [bones] from the former count.

*Uddhāra* (extraction) is the resolution of an objection such as the rejection of the commencement of the treatise. For instance, starting with the words "O Blessed One, some are seen... and so forth, when the objection is raised that "therefore the result of the distinction between the beneficial and the harmful is uncertain," the rebuttal is that "medical treatment and non-treatment cannot possibly be equal."

"Sambhava" means arising; that is, when something arises from this [cause] even though it was not explicitly taught. For example, it was stated: "Just as, through the removal of vitiated blood, there is the immediate pacification of the pain of hemorrhoids. That [pacification] occurs elsewhere as well, even in cases such as hornets, leeches, and so forth.
